titre_video: How a 25-Year-Old AI Boy Genius Lost $35 BILLION in 72 Hours

segments.titre: Hook: $35 billion gone in days
segments.resume: A 25-year-old AI whizz kid watched $35 billion vanish, hunted and harvested by a Wall Street predator in 24 hours using a forgotten financial loophole. The money was not the biggest prize, as the future of AI went with it too.
segments.texte: $35 billion… gone in a heartbeat. That was the exact number an AI whizz kid watched vanish from his bank account. He didn’t lose it. He didn’t spend it. It was hunted, harvested, by a predator. A Wall Street predator. All it took was 24 hours and a forgotten financial loophole to hijack a multi-billion dollar empire. But the money wasn’t the biggest prize. The future of AI went with it too.

segments.titre: Late July 2026: Aschenbrenner's wedding week
segments.resume: In late July 2026, 25-year-old Leopold Aschenbrenner ran one of the most celebrated hedge funds and was days from marrying Avital Balwit, chief of staff to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Instead of enjoying the best week of his life, he sat in a conference room negotiating a fire sale.
segments.texte: In late July 2026, Silicon Valley was gearing up for the tech wedding of the year. At 25, Leopold Aschenbrenner had it all. He ran one of the most celebrated hedge funds on earth and was days away from getting married to Avital Balwit, the chief of staff to Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic. It should be the best week of his life. Should have.

segments.titre: Three banks issue margin calls
segments.resume: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America simultaneously issued margin calls on his fund's positions, the lenders calling in the bill at the worst moment. To meet the calls he needed money by the market open the next morning.
segments.texte: Instead of enjoying himself and his guests, Leopold was buried in a conference room, negotiating the fire sale of his brief life’s work. It all started when three banks, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, and Bank of America, simultaneously issued margin calls on his fund’s positions. The people who lent him the cash to make bigger and bigger bets just called in the bill. At the worst possible moment. To meet those calls, Leopold needed money. And he needed it by the market open the next morning.

segments.titre: Anthropic stake search fails; Citadel takes the whole book
segments.resume: Aschenbrenner spent days trying to sell part of his Anthropic stake to roughly 10 parties, but no deal closed. The next morning his whole public equity portfolio, longs and shorts, was transferred to Citadel Securities in a pre-market block trade at a 10% discount to Ken Griffin.
segments.texte: He’d spent days trying to sell a piece of his stake in Anthropic privately, reportedly shopping the position to roughly 10 different parties. No deal closed. By now, he was out of options. When the sun came up the next day, every stock, long position, and short in his public equity portfolio was gone. Transferred to Citadel Securities in a single pre-market block trade. Ken Griffin had bought it all at a 10% discount.

segments.titre: Stocks rebound; Citadel's best month; 'best day of my life'
segments.resume: By the end of that day the dumped stocks were bouncing back, with CoreWeave up 22% and Bloom Energy up 26%, and Citadel posted its best month in years. Leopold posted that it was the best day of his life, meaning his wedding, while his fund had lost about $35 billion in under a week.
segments.texte: By the end of that day, stocks that Leopold had been forced to dump were already bouncing back. CoreWeave, one of his central positions, jumped 22%. Bloom Energy surged to 26%. The assets he’d sold in a panic to meet margin calls had immediately been repriced to what they were actually worth. Citadel was able to post its best month in years. That weekend, Leopold posted to his X account that he was having, “The best day of my life.” He was talking about his wedding. All while his fund had just lost about $35 billion in under a week.

segments.titre: How did a 25-year-old get that much money?
segments.resume: The video asks how a 25-year-old came to manage so much money and why lenders thought it reasonable, noting he built one of the largest hedge funds on earth in under two years and should never have been allowed near other people's money.
segments.texte: How did a 25-year-old get that much in the first place? And why did the people who gave it to him think that was a reasonable thing to do? Leopold built one of the largest hedge funds on earth in just under 2 years. He should never have been allowed near other people’s money in the first place.

segments.titre: Prodigy background: Columbia, Oxford and FTX Future Fund
segments.resume: Leopold Aschenbrenner, born in 2001, enrolled at Columbia at 15 and graduated valedictorian at 19 in economics and mathematics-statistics, with a professor citing a scholarship record unmatched in 20 years. He researched existential risk at Oxford, then spent nine months at Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX Future Fund, resigning the day the empire collapsed at age 20.
segments.texte: Leopold Ashchenbrenner was born in 2001. He enrolled at Columbia University at 15 since his academic record was genuinely that remarkable. A Columbia economics professor later described his work as having a “record of scholarship that exceeds that of any student in the department in the previous 20 years." He graduated valedictorian at 19 with degrees in economics and mathematics-statistics. Right out of Columbia, he went to Oxford to conduct research on existential risk. Then, he landed at FTX Future Fund, Sam Bankman-Fried’s philanthropic arm. He was there for 9 months, resigning on the day the whole empire collapsed. He watched the fraud unfold in real time. At close range. From the inside. He was 20 years old.

segments.titre: OpenAI Superalignment and the 2024 firing
segments.resume: Aschenbrenner joined OpenAI's Superalignment team in 2023, tasked with keeping AI from destroying civilization. In April 2024 he was fired, with OpenAI claiming he leaked confidential information while he said a security memo to the board about foreign espionage risks was the real reason.
segments.texte: A lesser person might have taken that experience and gone into something boring. Leopold went straight to OpenAI. He joined their “Superalignment” team in 2023, a group tasked with figuring out how to keep AI systems from destroying civilization. Depending on your perspective, that’s either the most important job in the world or a thought experiment with a very nice salary. In April 2024, he got fired. OpenAI claimed he leaked confidential information. Leopold argued back, publicly stating he had written a security memo to the board warning about foreign espionage risks. According to him, that was what actually got him pushed out.

segments.titre: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead
segments.resume: Two months later he published the 165-page Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, claiming AGI would arrive by 2027, run autonomous AI research and cascade into superintelligence within years, triggering a China and Russia geopolitical race. He presented it as fact without hedging, as if he had seen the future.
segments.texte: Two months later, Leopold published a document called Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead. It was 165 pages long. It was his driving thesis, the flag he hoped to plant in an industry he’d quickly come to dominate. It claimed that AGI, or Artificial General Intelligence, the kind that can do anything a human would do, would arrive by 2027. It would be capable of running autonomous AI research on its own. After that would come a cascade of superintelligence in a matter of years. China and Russia would enter a geopolitical race to keep pace. It would lead to a civilizational reckoning that would make every other event in human history look like child’s play. Leopold didn’t make a big point to do much “hedging” in his think piece. He didn’t qualify his statements with “perhaps” and “maybe.” He presented the whole thing as fact. As though he had seen the future and was frustrated that nobody else could see it yet.

segments.titre: Timing of the essay: a warning from the inside
segments.resume: The essay came weeks after his firing and two weeks before OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever resigned, so it hit the industry like a warning from someone who knew where the bodies were buried. When a document goes viral in Silicon Valley it gets read and then monetized.
segments.texte: The timing also made it impossible to dismiss as the work of a random blogger. He'd published it weeks after being fired from the most important AI lab in the world. It was also 2 weeks before Ilya Sutskever, one of OpenAI's co-founders, resigned from the company. Intentional or not, it hit the industry like a warning from the inside, written by someone who knew where the bodies were buried. When a document goes viral in Silicon Valley, it tends to get read… Then monetized.

segments.titre: Investors line up; critics call it a pitch deck
segments.resume: Wealthy, connected people wanted in, reasoning that if AGI was 18 months away whoever owned AI infrastructure in 2024 would own the world in 2027. Critics noted the essay and fund launch coincided, calling it visionary entrepreneurship or a sophisticated pitch deck dressed up as philosophy.
segments.texte: Very wealthy, very connected people began reaching out. They wanted in on whatever Leopold was about to do. If he was right, if AGI was just 18 months away, then whoever owned the right AI infrastructure assets in 2024 would own the world in 2027. Certain critics noticed that the essay and the fund launch all happened at the exact same time. If you scrutinize these things for a living, it seemed sketchy. Leopold essentially published a manifesto arguing that certain AI infrastructure investments were guaranteed to appreciate massively. Then he immediately launched a fund to make those investments… and asked the readers to hand over their money. To some it was visionary entrepreneurialism. To others it was an incredibly sophisticated pitch deck dressed up as philosophy.

segments.titre: Situational Awareness LP launches with $225 million
segments.resume: In September 2024 Situational Awareness LP launched with about $225 million in seed capital and a who's-who investor list. Leopold was 23 with no professional investing experience, only wealthy backers' money and unshakeable conviction.
segments.texte: In September 2024, Situational Awareness LP launched with approximately $225 million in seed capital. The investor list read like a who’s-who of the tech world. At the time, Leopold was still just 23-years-old. He had no professional investing experience. All he had were the purse strings to some very wealthy investors, and an unshakeable conviction that he could see where the world was headed.

segments.titre: The strategy and the spectacular returns
segments.resume: For about two years it looked like he was right: he went long AI hardware such as semiconductors and data center infrastructure and short software companies that had not monetized AI. The fund outperformed the S&P 500 about 8 times in its first year and by end of June 2026 was up 439% net since inception.
segments.texte: For about 2 years it looked like he was right. The fund’s strategy was anything but subtle. Leopold went long on AI hardware: the semiconductors, data center infrastructure, and machinery propping up the AI Revolution. He was short on software companies who had not figured out how to monetize it. This all-in-all-out strategy was a high-risk approach to building a hedge fund. It was one that would have gotten a traditional fund manager laughed out of the room. But for Aschenbrenner, it worked… Spectacularly. In the first year, the fund outperformed the S&P 500 by roughly 8 times. Then it kept going. By the end of June 2026, Situational Awareness LP was up by 439% net since inception.

segments.titre: How 4x leverage turns gains and losses
segments.resume: With 4x leverage, borrowing $300 to control $400 of positions on $100, a 25% gain becomes 100% but a 25% loss wipes out everything. Leopold reportedly used up to 400% leverage on some positions, borrowing $4 for every $1 he owned.
segments.texte: Then there was the leverage. If you have $100 and want to control $400 worth of positions, you borrow the other $300. At 4 time leverage, what Leopold’s fund was reported using, a 25% gain turns into a 100% gain. That’s the beauty of the system. But a 25% loss wipes out 100% of your assets. Every penny is gone. Leopold was reportedly using up to 400% leverage on some of his fund’s positions. In practice, that means he’d borrowed $4 for every $1 he owned. As long as the market kept going up, he’d look like the greatest investor alive. It’s the type of leverage that turns good returns into legendary returns.

segments.titre: $45 billion with eight employees versus Citadel's 3,000
segments.resume: Investors including Jane Street flooded in, and by July 1, 2026 the fund had about $45 billion in assets, up 1000% since launch, run from a small office with 8 employees. By contrast Ken Griffin's Citadel has about 3,000 people with risk teams and compliance, which Leopold decided he did not need.
segments.texte: Investors flooded in, making his positions even bigger. Even Jane Street, one of the most sophisticated trading firms in the world, joined the investing spree. By July 1st, 2026, the fund had approximately $45 billion in assets under management. That meant it had grown 1000% since it launched. All of this out of a small office with 8 employees. For context, Ken Griffin’s Citadel fund employs roughly 3,000 people. His firm is packed with risk teams, compliance infrastructure, and quantitative systems built over the decades. Leopold decided he didn’t need any of that. Or at least, he didn’t know he did. Besides, he had a thesis, a group chat, and a great deal of borrowed money.

segments.titre: Structural flaw: both legs bet on the same thesis
segments.resume: His long-short fund bought AI winners and shorted AI losers, so both sides paid off only if AI delivered, and doubts about AI's timeline would lose money on both legs at once, making it one enormous bet. His team was controlling rather than managing $45 billion, much of it borrowed and repayable on demand.
segments.texte: There was also a crucial structural problem in Leopold’s portfolio. He styled his fund as a long-short hedge fund. He bought the stocks that he thought would win the AI revolution and shorted the ones he thought would lose it. Both sides of his portfolio hinged on the same thesis. Basically, his long positions on semiconductor and infrastructure companies paid off if AI delivered. His short positions against software companies also paid off if AI delivered. But the moment the market started questioning whether AI would arrive on schedule, it would collapse. He'd lose money on both legs at once. From that perspective, it all looked like one enormous unhinged bet. In many ways, it was. Also, Leopold’s small team was not managing $45 billion at all. They were controlling it. A vast chunk of that was borrowed. It was money that all had to be returned on demand the moment the lenders got nervous.

segments.titre: David Cahn's $600 Billion Question
segments.resume: In July 2024 Sequoia partner David Cahn published AI's $600 Billion Question: Nvidia data center revenue of about $150 billion and about $300 billion of cloud AI spending required almost $600 billion in annual AI revenue at 50% gross margin, with a Goldman economist putting the gap near a trillion. If revenue did not catch up, the infrastructure thesis would be a costly collective hallucination.
segments.texte: While Leopold was riding the AI wave, a Sequoia Capital partner named David Cahn had been doing some math at a hedge fund holiday party. In July of 2024, the month after Leopold published his manifesto, Cahn published his own analysis with a provocatively simple title: “AI’s $600 Billion Question.” It was simple. Nvidia’s data center revenue was running at roughly $150 billion annually. Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft, the big cloud companies, were spending roughly $300 billion building out their AI infrastructure. To recoup that spending on a 50% gross margin, the industry needed to generate almost $600 billion in AI revenue. Every year. At the time, AI revenues across the entire industry was a mere fraction of that. A Goldman Sachs economist cited in the same analysis put the gap even higher, closer to a trillion dollars. That gap was the entire bet for big tech investors. If AI revenue eventually caught up to the infrastructure spend, Leopold’s massive plays would be vindicated. But if it didn’t, if the tech arrived too slowly or not at all, then the whole infrastructure thesis was nothing more than one of the most expensive collective hallucinations in financial history.

segments.titre: Leopold disagrees and borrows $4 for every $1
segments.resume: Leopold knew Cahn's argument and disagreed, believing AI would develop fast enough to generate the revenue, and he was so confident that he borrowed $4 for every dollar he owned. He declared war on the possibility of being wrong and doubled down.
segments.texte: Leopold knew this argument, and disagreed with it. He believed that AI would develop fast enough to generate the revenue to justify the spend. He was so confident that he borrowed $4 dollars for every dollar he owned to express that view. He declared war against the possibility of being wrong… and doubled down on where he felt he was right.

segments.titre: 17 July 2026: Meta Compute triggers the AI infrastructure selloff
segments.resume: On July 17, 2026 Meta announced Meta Compute, raising fears that tech giants were pulling back or restructuring AI data center spending, and the AI infrastructure complex sold off. Bloom Energy, SK Hynix, CoreWeave, Nebius and Sandisk, central positions of the fund, fell, and the portfolio dropped 35% that month.
segments.texte: The beginning of the end arrived on July 17, 2026. Meta announced something called “Meta Compute,” a new cloud-based infrastructure initiative that raised concerns. It had traders questioning whether tech giants were pulling back on AI data center spending or restructuring in ways that would benefit some companies and devastate others. Soon, the AI infrastructure complex started selling off. It felt more like a correction than a crash, but this is exactly the type of thing markets do. Bloom Energy declined sharply; then SK Hynix dropped, followed by CoreWeave, Nebius Group, Sandisk. These were the central pillars of Situational Awareness’ portfolio, which fell by 35% that month.

segments.titre: A 35% drop at 4x leverage means insolvency
segments.resume: A 35% decline on an unleveraged portfolio is painful but survivable, but at 4x leverage the equity is gone and the fund is technically insolvent on those positions. The banks that lent the other 75% no longer care about the AGI thesis and want their money back.
segments.texte: A 35% decline on an unleveraged portfolio is painful. You lose money, but you hold on. You wait for the recovery to eventually come. A 35% decline at 4 time leverage means your equity is all gone. You are technically insolvent on these positions. The banks who lent the other 75% of the money are no longer interested in your thesis about AGI and the decade ahead. They just want their money back.

segments.titre: The 'ructions' letter and the investor appeal
segments.resume: On July 24 Aschenbrenner sent investors a letter calling the turmoil ructions, describing the selloff as a buying opportunity and inviting fresh cash on August 1. His fund was in freefall, his wedding a week away, and he was still trying to keep investors appeased.
segments.texte: On July 24, Aschenbrenner sent a letter to investors describing the carnage using the word “ructions.” He called the selloff a buying opportunity and added a postscript inviting investors to put fresh cash into the fund on August 1st. It was a tough phase for him. His fund was in freefall. His wedding was in a week. And he was still fighting to keep the investors appeased.

segments.titre: Rivals short the stocks he must dump
segments.resume: A feedback loop formed as word spread of forced selling: competitors shorted the same stocks they knew Leopold would have to dump. When his team called rivals to offload positions, describing the book as hedges in distress, the rivals saw no hedges, just large directional bets blowing up.
segments.texte: The situation was made worse by a feedback loop that the fund’s rivals were actively accelerating. When word spread on Wall Street that a large fund was facing forced selling, competitors began shorting the same stocks they knew Leopold would have to dump. They’d try to drive the prices lower, and collect the profit when he inevitably sold. Leopold's team reportedly started calling rival funds to offload positions, describing the book as "a portfolio of hedges that were simply in distress." The rivals opened the file and immediately saw there were no hedges. Just large directional bets blowing up in real time. At that point Leopold was fighting the market. Everyone in it who could smell the margin call coming.

segments.titre: 29 July: lows, prime brokers' margin calls and the Anthropic stake sale attempt
segments.resume: By July 29 all core holdings hit 2026 lows at once and three prime brokers delivered margin calls, forcing liquidation. Leopold approached about 10 parties, including Sequoia and Greenoaks, to sell about $3.5 billion of his $5 billion Anthropic stake, but the banks began marketing chunks of the fund's positions before market open.
segments.texte: By July 29th, all of Leopold’s core holdings had hit 2026 lows simultaneously. That’s when his 3 prime brokers came delivering their margin calls. When multiple banks demand their money back at the same time, there’s only one option. Liquidate. Leopold was scrambling. He approached roughly 10 parties about selling a portion of his Anthropic stake. It was about $3.5 billion worth of a $5 billion holding. A desperate bid to raise the liquidity he urgently needed. Sequoia and Greenoaks were among those contacted. But a deal couldn’t come together fast enough. The banks started marketing chunks of the fund's positions to other players before market open, a signal that the fund was about to be involuntarily dismantled. That's when the phones started ringing.

segments.titre: Ken Griffin's playbook: Amaranth and Sowood
segments.resume: Ken Griffin founded Citadel in 1990 and it manages about $71 billion. He had done this before: Citadel bought the portfolio of Amaranth Advisors after its $6.4 billion natural gas loss in 2006, and took part of Sowood Capital's portfolio in 2007 during the subprime crisis.
segments.texte: Ken Griffin knew the market inside out. He founded Citadel in 1990, and today the firm manages approximately $71 billion in assets. Most importantly, he had played this game before. In 2006, Amaranth Advisors, a hedge fund that made spectacularly leveraged bets on natural gas futures, lost $6.4 billion in a matter of weeks. Citadel bought the portfolio. In 2007, during the early stages of the subprime crisis, a fund called Sowood Capital ran into trouble and had to transfer a portion of its portfolio to Citadel. The founder later said: "Citadel offered the only immediate and comprehensive solution."

segments.titre: Open auction for the book: Citadel, Jane Street, Millennium
segments.resume: Citadel, Jane Street and Millennium Management jumped in, creating an open auction for Leopold's book that Griffin won with the best bid. Jane Street, one of Leopold's own investors, bid on the remains, which the video calls just business.
mots_cles: investor bidding on its own fund
segments.texte: When Leopold’s AI fund was collapsing, Citadel, along with Jane Street and Millennium Management all jumped into the breach. It was essentially an open auction for the right to buy Leopold’s book. Griffin bid best, and won. Jane Street, who was also bidding, was ironically one of Leopold’s own investors. The same firm that had put money into Situational Awareness showed up at the fire sale to bid on its remains. That’s Wall Street. It’s just business.

segments.titre: The 10% discount and Citadel's $1.6 billion edge
segments.resume: Griffin is a buyer, not a rescuer, and Citadel's team pulled an all-nighter to find the price that guaranteed a profit, concluding 10% below market value. On about $16 billion of public equities that meant an immediate $1.6 billion profit before CoreWeave, Bloom Energy and others jumped over 20% the next day.
segments.texte: Ken Griffin is a buyer, not a rescuer, and buyers buy at the lowest possible price. The rules of a crisis transaction are not the same as the rules of a normal market transaction. When Citadel’s team pulled their all-nighter examining the Situational Awareness portfolio, the execs were trying to figure out what they’d need to pay to guarantee themselves a profit… Regardless of what happened next. They all knew the underlying companies within the portfolio itself were pretty sound bets. The answer was 10% below market value. If the fund held about $16 billion in public equities at the time of the sale, Citadel would walk away with an immediate $1.6 billion profit. That was before the stocks bounced, and CoreWeave, Bloom Energy, and others surged by over 20% the next trading day. The move gave Citadel its best month ever.

segments.titre: The irony: the thesis wasn't wrong
segments.resume: Citadel had its best month ever, and the assets Leopold was forced to sell were almost certainly going to recover. His AI infrastructure thesis was not wrong, but he was so aggressively leveraged that a temporary decline wiped him out.
segments.texte: And the ironic part? The assets Leopold had been forced to sell were almost certainly going to recover. His thesis about AI infrastructure wasn't wrong. He was just leveraged so aggressively that a temporary decline was enough to wipe him out.

segments.titre: Recklessness or deliberate squeeze? Griffin broke no rules
segments.resume: The video asks whether the liquidation was Leopold's recklessness or whether others knew he was vulnerable and accelerated his collapse, noting major hedge funds were deleveraging tech positions in the days before. That is not illegal or technically market manipulation, and Wall Street favors those with more information, capital, experience and leverage.
segments.texte: The question that keeps circulating in financial circles is whether Leopold's liquidation was the product of his own recklessness? Or were there people in the market who knew he was vulnerable and deliberately accelerated his collapse. Major hedge funds were rapidly deleveraging technology positions in the days immediately before the Situational Awareness forced liquidation. It’s not illegal at all. It’s not market manipulation, technically. But the timing is what it is. Ken Griffin broke zero rules. Wall Street simply systematically favors people who have more information, more capital, more experience, and more leverage.

segments.titre: What actually collapsed: the public book, not the fund
segments.resume: The real story is that the fund did not collapse; the public portfolio did. Leopold still holds his private Anthropic stake of about $5 billion, untouchable by margin calls and expected to grow at an IPO, and the fund still manages about $10 billion and is up overall, while recent investors, including those from July 1, were wiped out.
segments.texte: Most headlines are missing the real story. The fund itself didn’t collapse. What did collapse was Leopold's public portfolio. What remains was the thing he actually cared about the most: His stock in Anthropic, valued at approximately $5 billion. That stake was private, couldn't be touched by the margin calls, and is expected to become dramatically more valuable when Anthropic IPOs. His fund still manages approximately $10 billion, and by any one measure, it’s still up. The early investors are still sitting on an extraordinary amount of gains, despite the complete implosion of his public book. The people who were wiped out are the investors who allocated capital most recently, including anyone who got in on July 1st. They rode the leverage all the way up and then watched it crater in a single month.

segments.titre: Silicon Valley's reaction: a buying opportunity
segments.resume: Two weeks after the collapse Elad Gil asked to invest in the reconstituted fund and Sequoia partner Pat Grady told Bloomberg Leopold would be a fixture in Silicon Valley for a long time. Losing two-thirds of a fund in a month is a career-defining catastrophe on Wall Street but a buying opportunity in Silicon Valley.
segments.texte: Two weeks after the collapse, venture investor Elad Gil announced that he had requested to invest in the reconstituted fund. Pat Grady, a partner at Sequoia, told Bloomberg that Leopold would be "a fixture in Silicon Valley for a long time to come." On Wall Street, losing two-thirds of your fund in a month is a career-defining catastrophe. In Silicon Valley, it's a buying opportunity.

segments.titre: $400 million into one private startup days later
segments.resume: Days after Citadel bought his public book, Leopold wired $400 million of the fund's remaining capital into a single privately held startup, on top of $100 million invested a month earlier. The man nearly destroyed by one concentrated bet marked the occasion with another.
segments.texte: Days after Citadel bought his collapsing public book on a midnight fire sale, Leopold wired $400 million of the fund's remaining capital into a single privately held startup. That was on top of the $100 million he'd put into the same company just a month earlier. The man who had just been nearly destroyed by one enormous concentrated bet marked the occasion by making another one.

segments.titre: Silicon Valley's superpower and fatal flaw
segments.resume: Silicon Valley refuses to let a dramatic failure be the last one, so a $35 billion detour in your mid-20s is just a plot point, and Ken Griffin has been doing this since 1987. There is a lot riding on the AI revolution, with many people standing to make money, but the video asks whether it is a gamble worth making.
segments.texte: This is Silicon Valley's superpower. And its fatal flaw. It is a complete refusal to let a dramatic failure be the last one. In a world obsessed with trillion-dollar outcomes, a $35 billion detour in your mid-t20 is just a plot point. Ken Griffin has been doing this since 1987. He probably agrees. There’s a lot riding on the AI revolution… and a lot of people stand to make a lot of money. But is it a gamble worth making?
